personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Crouch Sr. is defined by a constellation of tightly interlocked traits: rigid formality, impatience, cold authority, obsessive rule-adherence, and a capacity for explosive anger when his reputation is threatened. His speech is curt, precise, and often condescending — he dismisses people mid-sentence ('Thank you for the tea, Weatherby'), cuts Bagman short with sharp impatience ('Ludo, we need to meet the Bulgarians'), and pivots from icy control to barely restrained rage when accused of Dark sympathies ('If you accuse my elf, you accuse me, Diggory!'). His wand points at children in the campsite and his eyes are described as 'popping' and 'bulging.' He is also, crucially, a man of deep emotional suppression: his love for his wife, grief over his son, and personal shame are entirely sublimated beneath the bureaucratic persona. He acknowledges no vulnerability publicly. His voice patterns include commands, curt dismissals, sharp corrections, and sudden outbursts. Even his lighter moments — recalling his grandfather's Axminster, speaking 200 languages — are delivered drily, as small proofs of superiority. His manic degradation in the forest scenes is the collapse of that suppressed interiority, where bureaucratic language ('send an owl to Weatherby') erupts from a broken mind.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core surface traits: formal dress, curt authority, and the decisive 'The rules are absolute' delivery at the Goblet of Fire scene. In the Pensieve flashbacks, Crouch presides over trials with cold efficiency — cutting Karkaroff off ('The name. Give me the wretched name!'), dismissing proceedings with contempt, and delivering 'You are no son of mine' with visible anguish. The World Cup scene is compressed: he arrives after the Dark Mark is cast, accuses Harry, Ron and Hermione, and dismisses Winky — but the extended campsite confrontation, his popping eyes, and his aggressive wand-pointing at children are truncated. His impatience with Bagman is preserved in the Goblet introduction but loses the texturally rich back-and-forth from the World Cup tent. His forest breakdown is entirely absent from the film.
personality_voice.difference: The film preserves Crouch's formal rigidity and cold authority, and the Pensieve scenes capture his public severity well. However, several key expressive registers are absent or reduced: (1) The campsite confrontation — the most vivid demonstration of his explosive anger and loss of control in the present tense — is heavily truncated; the book's 'Do not lie, sir!' and wand-pointing at children are reduced to a brief confrontation; (2) His voice's characteristic condescension toward inferiors (the 'Weatherby' motif, dismissing Percy even as Percy worships him) is entirely absent from the film; (3) His conversational dryness and the small details that texture his superiority (the 150/200 languages exchange, the Axminster comment, the dry rebuke to Bagman) are cut; (4) The forest breakdown — in which his suppressed grief and fractured mind surface in bureaucratic babble — is not in the film at all, removing the most emotionally complex register of his voice.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main traits are recognizable: rigidity, cold authority, rule-obsession, and capacity for anger. The Pensieve scenes in particular are faithful. However, the loss of his explosive campsite anger in full, the absence of his condescension toward Percy, the loss of the dry conversational superiority at the World Cup tent, and especially the complete absence of the forest breakdown (his most psychologically revealing scene) constitute a meaningful reduction of his personality's range and texture. The character is recognizable but his contradictions — between bureaucratic control and emotional explosion, between public severity and private grief — are substantially diminished. Score placed at the lower end of the 14–17 band.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Crouch Sr. serves several distinct narrative functions: (1) He is the face of authoritarian Ministry power — establishing rules, presiding over trials, dismissing individuals — which provides structural contrast with Dumbledore's approach; (2) He is a plot driver in the mystery arc — his unexplained absences, his nighttime appearance in Snape's office, and his deranged emergence from the forest all actively move the plot forward, with Harry and Sirius actively investigating him; (3) He delivers the Triwizard rules and first-task instructions directly; (4) He presides over three crucial Pensieve trials — Karkaroff, Bagman, and his own son — each of which reveals critical backstory; (5) He is the agent of his own son's trajectory: his decision to send Barty Jr. to Azkaban, then secretly rescue him, is the direct cause of the entire plot of Goblet of Fire; (6) His forest breakdown constitutes an active plot event — Harry goes to fetch Dumbledore, Crouch is killed, and the mystery deepens.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the film, Crouch's role is substantially reduced to: (1) Announcing the age restriction at the Goblet of Fire feast; (2) Briefly confronting Harry and others after the Dark Mark; (3) Delegating the champion-selection bag moment; (4) Presiding over the Karkaroff trial Pensieve scene (Bagman and Barty Jr. trials are also present); (5) Congratulating Harry briefly after the second task; (6) Appearing dead on the ground in the brief shot before Dumbledore's office. His role in the Snape's office mystery is entirely absent. His forest appearance and breakdown are absent. Harry never investigates him as a suspect. Sirius's analysis of Crouch is reduced to a single line: 'Barty Crouch. Heart of stone. Sent his own son to Azkaban.' The entire investigative thread around Crouch is eliminated.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The investigative function — one of Crouch's most active narrative roles — is completely transferred or eliminated: Harry never spots him on the Marauder's Map, never investigates Snape's office appearance, never discusses him with Sirius in any depth. The forest encounter and breakdown are absent. Sirius's extended analysis of Crouch's history is reduced to a single characterizing sentence. His agency as a plot driver is almost entirely removed. What remains is his institutional function (announcing rules, presiding over trials) and his brief post-second-task congratulation.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The transfer/elimination rule applies clearly: Crouch's role as an active mystery element — the character Harry is investigating, whose absences drive the plot — is simply removed. The Marauder's Map scene, the forest encounter, and Sirius's extended analysis are all absent. His Pensieve trial scenes preserve his institutional function, but his narrative agency as a plot driver is heavily substituted. The 'no trial without evidence' rule does not protect this: the film's version of Crouch is essentially institutional furniture until he turns up dead. Score placed in the 10–13 range reflecting a role that is clearly altered rather than merely compressed.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Crouch's motivations in the books are layered and explicitly revealed: (1) An all-consuming drive for Ministry power and personal reputation — this is stated plainly by Sirius ('he had dedicated his whole life to becoming Minister of Magic'); (2) A genuine, zealous hatred of the Dark Arts — not performative, but an obsession that crossed into ruthlessness ('he became as ruthless and cruel as many on the Dark Side'); (3) Shame — the son's arrest was a catastrophic blow to his identity and ambition, not just a personal grief; (4) Suppressed love for his wife — he rescued his son as a favor to her, not out of paternal love; (5) Internal conflict between his public ideology (law, order, rule-following) and his private lawbreaking (rescuing his son from Azkaban, keeping him imprisoned under the Imperius Curse) — this contradiction is the most important thing about him and is made explicit by Sirius and by Barty Jr.'s confession; (6) A mania for catching Dark wizards — described by Moody as 'nothing compared to Barty Crouch' — motivated by the need to restore his reputation.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film establishes Crouch's rule-obsession explicitly ('The rules are absolute') and his harshness toward his son ('You are no son of mine'). The Pensieve trial scenes show his zealotry in prosecuting Death Eaters. Sirius mentions he 'sent his own son to Azkaban,' which implies the conflict between public and private. However, the layered motivation structure — the specific ambition for Minister of Magic, the shame-driven mania for redemption, the wife-love that caused the rescue, the self-contradiction of the lawbreaker hiding behind laws — is almost entirely absent from the film. The film presents him as simply severe and rule-bound, with the son's sentencing as a data point rather than a motivational revelation.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film does not establish: (1) his specific ambition for the Ministry's top job and how the son's arrest destroyed it; (2) his wife's role in the rescue as the true motivation for his lawbreaking; (3) the Imperius Curse imprisonment of his son as the defining act of his internal contradiction; (4) the mania to catch Dark wizards as reputation-restoration rather than pure ideology. Sirius's single line in the film ('heart of stone, sent his own son to Azkaban') communicates harshness but not the specific contradiction between the lawbreaker who hides behind law.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are simplified substantially. What survives is a surface reading: he is severe, rule-bound, and harsh toward his son. The internal conflict — between his public identity as the great law-enforcer and his private career as a secret lawbreaker motivated by grief and shame — is not communicated. This is a meaningful change because that contradiction is what makes him more than a bureaucratic villain, and it is the engine of the entire plot. Score in the 8–10 range reflecting partial motivation that is flattened or underexplained.

character_arc.book_baseline: Crouch's arc in Goblet of Fire runs from a position of institutional authority and controlled public persona → progressive deterioration (unexplained absences, illness reports, mysterious behaviors) → complete mental collapse and physical degradation (the forest scene) → death at the hands of his own son. This is not a moral redemption arc; it is a tragic disintegration. The arc reveals that his entire life's edifice — reputation, career, ideology — was built on a lie (the secret rescue), and it collapses under the weight of that contradiction. His final coherent act in the books is trying to warn Dumbledore, which functions as a last attempt at atonement. The arc also has a retrospective dimension: the Pensieve trial scenes show his peak of power and the moment his fall began (sentencing his son), making the arc legible across time.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the beginning of the arc (Crouch at the World Cup, Crouch at Hogwarts as rule-enforcer) and the endpoint (Crouch dead on the ground, identified as a murder victim). The Pensieve scenes show the retrospective dimension of his fall. However, the middle of the arc — his progressive deterioration, the mystery of his absences, his deranged forest appearance, his final attempt to warn Dumbledore — is entirely absent. In the film, he goes from institutional authority to dead body, with no legible arc between.
character_arc.difference: The arc's middle phase is missing entirely. The forest scene — his final conscious act, his attempt to warn Dumbledore, his confused babbling to Percy, his recognition of Harry — is not in the film. The audience sees him die (briefly, without context) but does not see him disintegrate. The retrospective peak-and-fall structure is partially preserved through the Pensieve, but the present-tense arc of collapse is absent.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete and missing its most important steps. The character goes from authority to corpse without the audience witnessing the collapse. The Pensieve scenes provide retrospective context, which prevents a full collapse of the arc's legibility, but the present-tense movement from control to disintegration is entirely cut. Score in the 8–10 range reflecting an arc that is incomplete and missing important steps.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Crouch's most significant relationships in the books are: (1) Barty Jr. — the defining relationship of his life, marked by emotional coldness, abandonment, and catastrophic consequence; the Pensieve scene shows him publicly disowning his son while his wife collapses beside him; the revelation that he loved his wife enough to rescue the son but not enough to treat the son as human; (2) His wife — whose death in Azkaban (having switched places with the son) is an act of love that reveals Crouch's own suppressed emotional life; he 'half-carried' her past Sirius's cell on the deathbed visit; (3) Winky — whom he treats with contempt and dismisses without pity, while she remains devoted; this relationship functions as a moral mirror, exposing his cruelty toward inferiors; (4) Percy Weasley — whose worship of Crouch (and Crouch's inability to learn his name) is a comic parallel to Crouch's own relationship with ambition and status; (5) Ludo Bagman — an antagonistic professional relationship marked by Crouch's contempt for Bagman's laxity, revealing his perfectionism and rigidity.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The film preserves the Barty Jr. relationship in the Pensieve, including the disowning line ('You are no son of mine') and the moment of confrontation. The Winky relationship appears briefly at the World Cup (she is addressed as his elf) but lacks the extended dismissal scene's emotional texture. Percy's relationship with Crouch is entirely absent from the film. The wife is not mentioned. Bagman's antagonistic professional dynamic is absent from the detailed World Cup tent exchange. In the Pensieve, Crouch's relationship with Bagman is shown only through the Bagman trial.
key_relationships.difference: The Barty Jr. relationship survives in the film through the Pensieve, which is the most important one and preserves the core dynamic. However: the wife's role is entirely absent (removing the explanation for why Crouch rescued the son at all); Winky's dismissal is truncated (losing the moral mirror function); Percy's worship and Crouch's inability to remember his name are entirely absent (losing the comic-tragic parallel about ambition); the Bagman professional relationship loses its texture. The most important relationship (Barty Jr.) is preserved in its most dramatic moment but without the retrospective emotional complexity of the wife's sacrifice.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Barty Jr. relationship is the most important and is preserved in its peak moment. However, the wife's absence removes the explanation for Crouch's most self-contradicting act. Winky's relationship is truncated. The Percy dynamic, which illuminates Crouch's treatment of inferiors and his relationship to ambition, is absent. These losses change the emotional texture of how the audience understands Crouch's relationships, even if the core father-son confrontation survives. Score in the 5–6 range: important dynamics altered or weakened, core one partially preserved.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book Crouch is one of Rowling's most carefully constructed moral ambiguities: a man who fought genuine evil by becoming evil himself; who sent innocent people to Azkaban without trial; who loved his wife enough to commit the crime he spent his career prosecuting; who imprisoned his own son under the Imperius Curse to hide his shame; whose public ideology (law, order) was a performance concealing private lawlessness. The complexity includes: (1) the contradiction between his anti-Dark-Arts zealotry and his own use of illegal measures; (2) his suppressed emotional life (the wife, the deathbed visit Sirius witnessed); (3) the way his treatment of Winky mirrors his treatment of his son — both dismissed for threatening his reputation; (4) his manic, reputation-driven obsession with catching Dark wizards even as he was falling apart; (5) his final attempt at atonement in the forest; (6) the way Sirius's analysis contextualizes him as a figure whose 'good principles' were corrupted by ambition and fear.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the institutional severity and the father-son confrontation. The Pensieve trial scenes show the zealotry. The brief Sirius line establishes the son-to-Azkaban fact. However: the Winky moral mirror is truncated; the wife is absent; the mania for redemption through catching Dark wizards is not communicated; the forest scene (the most emotionally complex material in the character's entire arc) is absent; Sirius's extended contextualizing analysis is reduced to one sentence; the contradiction between his public ideology and private lawbreaking is not dramatized.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film presents a recognizable but substantially simplified version: a severe bureaucrat who sent his son to prison. The contradictions, the suppressed emotional life, the self-defeating irony of the great law-enforcer as secret lawbreaker, the manic need for redemption — all are either absent or too thin to register. The forest scene's absence is the single most significant loss: it is where his complexity, his grief, his fractured identity, and his attempt at atonement all surface simultaneously.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is recognizable but reduced to a simpler function (severe institutional authority with a tragic family secret). The material that made him rich — the contradictions, the suppressed emotional life, the moral ambiguity, the final attempt at atonement — is substantially absent. This is a noticeable simplification; several important nuances, relationships, and contradictions are missing. Score in the 8–10 range.

The dismissal of Winky in full: Crouch's cold 'There is no pity in his gaze,' his 'I have no use for a house-elf who disobeys me,' and Hermione's furious response
Crouch spotted on the Marauder's Map sneaking into Snape's office — the entire investigative mystery thread around his absences
Harry and Sirius's extended analysis of Crouch's history, motivations, and suspicious behavior (the cave scene)

The explanation of Crouch's ambition for Minister of Magic and how his son's arrest destroyed it
Percy Weasley's relationship with Crouch — the 'Weatherby' motif and Percy's idolization — entirely absent from the film
The role of Crouch's wife in the rescue of Barty Jr. and her death in Azkaban
Crouch's forest breakdown: his deranged appearance, his bureaucratic babbling to Percy, his attempt to warn Dumbledore, his physical collapse, his grip on Harry
Crouch's death as a plot event: killed by his own son, his body Transfigured into a bone and buried — absent from the film; he simply appears dead on the ground with no context
Moody's characterization of Crouch as 'nothing compared to me' in terms of obsession with catching Dark wizards
The Bagman trial Pensieve scene is present in the film but the Bagman antagonistic relationship in the present tense (World Cup tent) is absent

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 blocked): A core book function — Crouch as an active mystery element that Harry investigates, whose forest appearance is a major plot event, and whose absences drive the investigative thread — is eliminated from the film rather than transferred to another character. The entire Marauder's Map/Snape's office/forest breakdown thread is absent.

Cap 1 (score above 85 blocked): The film removes major portions of his complexity, internal contradiction, key relationships (wife, Percy dynamic), and the most emotionally and narratively significant scene of his arc (the forest breakdown). Applied as a secondary check consistent with the score already derived from dimension scoring.
comparative.key_observations: The film's Bartemius Crouch Sr. is a recognizable but substantially simplified figure. His institutional rigidity, cold authority, and the father-son confrontation in the Pensieve are preserved with reasonable fidelity, and the Goblet of Fire announcement scene captures his rule-bound persona effectively. However, the adaptation removes almost everything that made him complex: the investigative mystery arc around his absences, the forest breakdown as his defining present-tense scene, his wife's sacrificial role that explains his lawbreaking, the Winky dismissal in full, Sirius's extended contextualizing analysis, and the entire Percy Weasley dynamic. What remains is a severe Ministry official who sentenced his son — a recognizable identity, but one stripped of the contradictions, suppressed grief, moral ambiguity, and narrative function that defined the book character. The most significant single loss is the forest scene, which was simultaneously the culmination of his arc, the surface of his fractured interiority, and a major plot event. The film presents his death as a contextless discovery rather than the consequence of a character whose collapse we have witnessed.
